title: The moon days
hookLine: keeping the uposatha each full moon
tomorrow: Mai's mom asks: 'are you still you?' how would she even check?

lines: A PHOTO OF THE ALTAR: RẰM.
A DORM, A DEADLINE, MUSIC ON.
CAN THE MOON DAY BE KEPT HERE?
cards: Ông texts Mai a photo of the altar at home: fresh flowers, a bowl of fruit, and one word, rằm. Full moon. On the full and new moons he eats vegetarian and goes to the temple.
Mai is in a dorm far from home: no temple within walking distance, a roommate with music on, a studio deadline. Can a moon day be kept in a place like that?

teach.b: The suttas call these days uposatha: observance days at the full and new moons and the half moons between. Monks gather and recite their rules. Lay followers do something remarkable.

teach.h: EIGHT PRECEPTS, ONE DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: In one sutta, the Buddha describes them taking on eight precepts for a single day and night, the way the awakened ones live all the time: no killing, no stealing, no lying, no intoxicants, no sex, no food after noon, no shows, music or adornment, and no luxurious bed.
For one day, a householder lives close to a monk's life. Then, in another sutta, a laywoman named Visakha comes to the Buddha on a moon day, and he asks her which kind she's keeping.

teach.h: THE COWHERD'S KIND, OR THE NOBLE KIND.
teach.b: There's the cowherd's kind, he says: a man who spends the day thinking about where his cows will graze tomorrow, and what he'll eat tomorrow. Present in body, elsewhere in mind.
And there's the noble kind: a day spent cleansing the mind, remembering the Buddha, the teaching, the community, and keeping the precepts.
That's the teaching under every moon day. It isn't the building that makes it, or a perfect setting. It's what you take on, and what your mind is doing while you keep it.
A dorm works. A deadline works.
A day kept apart is kept from the inside.

how: On uposatha days at the moon's phases, monks recite their rules and some lay Buddhists visit the temple, listen to teachings and take the eight precepts for a day and a night; in Vietnamese families, the full and new moons of the lunar month are often kept with vegetarian meals and a temple visit.

o: observance days at the moon's phases, with extra precepts
festivals where Buddhists gather to watch the moon rise
nights of fasting kept only by monks and nuns

games.q: the moon day — tap the pairs.
p: the observance day at the moon's phases
kept for a day and a night
asked which kind she was keeping

s: the moon days are only for monks and nuns
lay followers keep them too, taking eight precepts for a day and a night.
on a moon day, lay followers may take on no food after noon
it's one of the eight precepts kept for that day and night.
keeping a moon day just means eating a vegetarian meal
food can be part of it, but the texts describe precepts taken on and a mind cleansed.

games.q: a coworker's family keeps the full moon, but she's stuck on a double shift that day. she figures she can't keep it this month. what fits the Buddha's words to Visakha?
o: keep what she can, in her conduct and her mind, even at work
skip the month; it only counts with a day off and a temple
make up for it by keeping two moon days next month instead
games.why: the noble kind of moon day is a mind cleansed and precepts kept, not a perfect setting. the cowherd was at the right place and missed it.

practice: Close your eyes and take on one small precept for the length of this sit: no reaching for the phone, no shifting for comfort, no grabbing for a snack or a song.
Keep it the whole time, the way a moon-day keeper keeps eight for a day and a night. Notice what the small no makes room for.

wordCard.voice: The moon days: uposatha, when lay Buddhists take on extra precepts for a day and a night, wherever they are.

orig.note: Pali: the observance day, kept at the moon's phases with precepts and teaching.

carryVoice: Carry this: a day kept apart, set by the moon and kept wherever you are. Moon's up.
